newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul says North Korean apology not good enough.
newsitem.headline: Seoul says North Korean apology not good enough.

text.p: South Korean President Kim Young-sam on Tuesday welcomed North Korea's apology for last September's submarine incursion but warned against raising hopes for peace, calling for "action rather than words" by Pyongyang.
In a New Year news conference, Kim urged the communist North to abandon its bellicose stand against the South and join peace talks with South Korea, the United States and China.
But he offered no new diplomatic initiatives in the news conference, which he normally uses for unveiling major policies.

"It is fortunate for peace and stability on the Korean peninsula that at the end of last year North Korea formally admitted and apologised for the incursion of a North Korean submarine into our waters and then pledged that no incursions will recur," he said.
"However, it is action, rather than words, that counts."
He said the incursion showed North Korea had not abandoned its dream of unifying Korea under communism. The peninsula was divided at the end of World War Two.
Kim said North Korea had agreed to attend a preparatory briefing this month on the four-nation peace talks jointly proposed by him and U.S. President Bill Clinton last year.
The briefing will be conducted by U.S. and South Korean officials.
"Within this month the three countries will meet for a briefing and we already have a promise from North Korea. But we don't know the time or the place yet," Kim said.
The session is designed to pave the way for talks aimed at securing a permanent peace arrangement on the Korean peninsula to replace a truce that ended the 1950-53 Korean War.
The move is part of growing contacts between North Korea and the West after Pyongyang apologised for the submarine incident.

The Shark-class submarine landed 26 armed agents on a Southern beach last September. North Korea apologised on December 29. The following day South Korea returned the bodies of 24 infiltrators shot dead during a manhunt.
One was captured alive and is in South Korean government custody. The other is still at large.
On Monday, the U.S. Treasury said it had given a licence to giant grain company Gargill to export 500,000 tonnes of food to famine-struck North Korea.
"It is significant in the sense that the United States has had a trade embargo" with North Korea, said Victor Cha, a Georgetown University professor who specialises in East Asian and Korean issues.
Kim said North Korea faced many internal problems and it was not time to talk of an inter-Korean summit to discuss major steps for reunification.
"The security situation on the Korean peninsula remains volatile and the instability of North Korea due to its increasing difficulties could threaten the peace," he said.
He said North Korea's economic problems and a severe energy shortage were reflected in crashes of planes which were flying with inadequate fuel.
"Three North Korean MiG fighters crashed in the past one month because of the shortage of fuel," he said.
